title: Smartphones, Social Media & Youth Mental Health
scope: Smartphones and social media as a cause of the youth mental-health decline.

overview.summary: Reported teen distress climbed after 2010; whether phones and platforms caused it, and what should follow, is contested.
overview.scope_covered: Youth distress since 2010: causal evidence, effect size, rival explanations, platform design, and access restrictions.
overview.scope_excluded: Adult users, early-childhood screen time, online sexual exploitation, and speech moderation beyond minors’ access.
overview.why_now: Restriction is outrunning agreement about what it does: Australia’s under-16 ban, the first national law of its kind, took effect on 10 December 2025, and platforms revoked access to about 4.7 million under-16 accounts in its first five weeks, before any study of what that changes for adolescent wellbeing.

basics.intro: Facts every camp works from: what the trend data actually show, how large the measured association is, how much exposure has changed, and how far restriction has already gone.

stats.label: Persistent sadness or hopelessness · teen girls, CDC survey
stats.note: 53% of US high school girls reported persistent sadness or hopelessness in 2023, versus 36% in 2011 and a peak of 57% in 2021.
stats.detail: The CDC’s Youth Risk Behavior Survey asks whether a student felt so sad or hopeless almost every day for two or more weeks in a row that they stopped some usual activities. The 2011 baselines come from the CDC’s own 2011 surveillance summary, which put the figure at 35.9% for girls and 21.5% for boys. Boys rose too, from 21.5% in 2011 to 29% in 2021, but the increase and the current level are markedly larger among girls. Levels dipped from 2021 to 2023 but remain far above the pre-2012 baseline.

series.source_label: CDC, Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance — United States, 2011 (MMWR Surveillance Summaries 61, no. 4)

stats.label: Suicide rate · ages 10 to 14 (CDC)
stats.note: The suicide rate for 10-to-14-year-olds roughly tripled between 2007 and 2018, from 0.9 to 2.9 deaths per 100,000 a year, then leveled off.
stats.detail: This is a hard mortality outcome recorded on death certificates, not a self-report survey item, so it is not affected by changing willingness to disclose distress. The broader 10-to-24 age group saw suicide rates rise 62% from 2007 to 2021, from 6.8 to 11.0 per 100,000. The rise begins around 2007 to 2009, a timing question positions read differently against smartphone and social media adoption curves.
stats.source_label: CDC National Center for Health Statistics, Data Brief No. 471

stats.label: Emergency room visits for self-harm · girls aged 10 to 14 (US)
stats.note: Self-harm ER visits among girls aged 10 to 14 climbed about 19% a year from 2009 to 2015, from about 110 to nearly 318 per 100,000; boys’ rates did not rise.
stats.detail: Drawn from a national injury-surveillance system, this is a hospital-record measure rather than a survey response, so it speaks to whether the rise in distress shows up in behavior as well as self-report. The uptick begins around 2009 and is sharpest in the youngest girls, a pattern later analyses have used to mark the shift’s starting point. Published in JAMA in 2017.

stats.label: Share of wellbeing differences linked to tech use · Orben & Przybylski (2019)
stats.note: Across three datasets covering about 355,000 teenagers, technology and social media use explained at most 0.4% of the variation in wellbeing.
stats.detail: Orben and Przybylski’s 2019 study in Nature Human Behaviour pooled three nationally representative datasets, the Youth Risk Behavior Survey, Monitoring the Future and the UK’s Millennium Cohort Study, about 355,000 adolescents in total, and ran a specification-curve or “multiverse” analysis: instead of reporting the single model a researcher happened to run first, it tests every defensible combination of predictors, outcomes and covariates, to show how much the result depends on analytic choices. Social media use specifically showed a somewhat larger negative association than digital technology use overall. The paper is a touchstone for the debate over whether population-average effects this small can still matter, or whether they mask larger effects concentrated in particular groups.

stats.label: Countries with rising school loneliness · PISA, 2012 to 2018
stats.note: School loneliness rose in 36 of 37 countries surveyed between 2012 and 2018, and the share of teens reporting high loneliness nearly doubled worldwide.
stats.detail: Twenge and colleagues (Journal of Adolescence, 2021) analyzed PISA data from over a million teens. In statistical models, loneliness was higher where smartphone and internet access were higher, but the design is correlational and cannot establish causation. A parallel cross-national series, the WHO’s Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, found no evidence of substantial declines in adolescent mental well-being across 36 countries from 2002 to 2018 (Cosma and colleagues, Journal of Adolescent Health, 2020), so the exact years and measures used affect what pattern shows up.

stats.label: Smartphone access · US teens aged 13 to 17 (Pew)
stats.note: 95% of US teens say they have a smartphone or can use one, up from about 73% a decade earlier.
stats.detail: Pew Research Center surveyed US teens ages 13 to 17 in September and October 2024. Access is slightly higher among older teens (98%) than younger teens (90%). Near-saturation of ownership shifts the practical debate from whether teens have devices to how much they use them and what platforms show them.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, Teens, Social Media and Technology 2024

stats.label: Teens online almost constantly · self-report (Pew)
stats.note: 40% of US teens say they are online almost constantly in 2025, up from 24% a decade earlier, though down slightly from 2024.
stats.detail: Pew’s 2025 survey found about 20% of teens report near-constant TikTok use, about 20% near-constant YouTube use, and 12% each for Instagram and Snapchat. This measures self-reported frequency of being online, not hours logged, and captures the shift from occasional checking to near-continuous connectivity that most positions treat as the relevant “dose.”
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, Teens, Social Media and AI Chatbots 2025

stats.label: States requiring districts to restrict school cellphone use · US
stats.note: As of 28 July 2026, at least 39 states and the District of Columbia require school districts to ban or restrict students’ cellphone use in schools (Education Week tally).
stats.detail: Education Week’s tracker counts states that require districts to act, and the category runs from bell-to-bell bans to instructional-time-only rules, so it is looser than a full-day ban implies: Illinois’ July 2026 law, for one, lets districts allow high school students to use phones at lunch and between classes; Florida’s 2023 law, among the earliest, is scoped to instructional time. Almost all of the movement has come since 2024, a rapid policy shift running well ahead of multi-year evidence on whether restrictions change measured mental-health outcomes; early evaluations mostly track discipline, phone confiscations and self-reported focus rather than depression or anxiety measures.

stats.label: Under-16 accounts removed · Australia’s social media law
stats.note: Australia’s under-16 law, the first of its kind, took effect on 10 December 2025; platforms cut off about 4.7 million accounts in its first five weeks.
stats.detail: The law covers ten platforms including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube and X, and requires ‘reasonable steps’ toward age assurance (document checks, biometric age estimation or behavioral signals) rather than one mandated method; non-compliant platforms face fines up to A$49.5 million. It is the first real-world, national-scale test of an access-restriction approach, and its effects on adolescent wellbeing have not yet been independently studied.
stats.source_label: Australian Government eSafety Commissioner (via PBS NewsHour)

stats.label: Children with current anxiety · US, ages 3 to 17
stats.note: 9.2% of US children aged 3 to 17 had a current anxiety diagnosis in 2020, up from 7.1% in 2016; depression rose from 3.1% to 4.0%.
stats.detail: Data are from the National Survey of Children’s Health, reported by parents as a condition a child has at the time of the survey rather than as a mood-scale response, published in JAMA Pediatrics. Anxiety rose 29% and depression 27% across the five years, a rise that predates the pandemic-era surveys most often cited. It bears on the “prevalence inflation” question from the other direction: a formal diagnosis requires provider contact, but rising diagnosis rates could still reflect more help-seeking and screening rather than only more underlying distress.

stats.label: Teens who call social media’s effect mostly negative · self-report (Pew)
stats.note: 48% of US teens say social media mostly hurts people their age, up from 32% in 2022, but only 14% say it mostly hurts them personally.
stats.detail: Pew’s survey also finds 45% of teens think they spend too much time on social media and 19% say it hurts their own mental health, against 44% of concerned parents who name social media as the top driver of teen mental health problems. The same survey records the other direction: 11% call the effect on peers mostly positive and 41% neither, only 14% say the effect on them personally is mostly negative, and on friendships more teens say these platforms help than hurt, 30% against 7%. The gap between what teens say about their peers and what they say about themselves recurs across the debate.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, 10 facts about teens and social media

stats.label: Sleep lost at high screen time · 9+ hours a day (cohort study)
stats.note: Fifteen-year-olds with 9 or more hours of daily screen time slept about 32 minutes less than peers under 2 hours, and were 60% more likely to report poor sleep.
stats.detail: From a Brazilian birth-cohort study (Sleep Medicine: X, 2023) covering roughly 1,900 adolescents; screen time here means entertainment use across TV, computers, gaming and phones, not social media specifically, and this estimate is not US-specific.

questions.text: Does adolescent social media use cause the post-2010 mental-health decline, or mostly move alongside it?
questions.why: The timing overlap is undisputed; whether one drove the other is not, because the same decade brought many other candidate causes that correlational data cannot separate out.
questions.detail:
Proponents of causation point to the tight international timing alignment between smartphone adoption curves and the distress curve, the biological plausibility of sleep and attention displacement, and school- or platform-access studies that sometimes show short-term mood effects. Skeptics counter that large longitudinal panels find associations too small to plausibly explain a decline this size, that the effects shrink or disappear under preregistered specifications, and that a shared decade-level trend is a weak causal instrument given how many other things changed at once.

The strongest pro-causation case is convergence: dose-response signals in some cohorts, gender and platform-specific patterns that track known design differences, and a cross-country pattern that follows smartphone penetration more closely than general internet access. The strongest rival case is effect-size math: Orben and Przybylski put technology use at no more than 0.4% of the variation in adolescent wellbeing, an association they argue is far too small to be the primary driver of a population-wide shift, and Candice Odgers argues in her 2024 Nature review that a wider set of causes, economic hardship, violence and the opioid epidemic among them, better explains the post-2010 trends.

questions.text: If effects exist, are they small and spread thin, or large and concentrated in particular ages and children?
questions.why: Averaged across all teens the measured effect looks tiny, but an average can hide a large harm concentrated in a few, so the same data reads as barely matters or matters enormously.
questions.detail:
The small-and-diffuse reading treats the modest average effect size as the number that should govern population-wide policy, arguing a small correlation replicated across huge samples is still a small correlation rather than a large one hiding in wait, and that slicing the data by age, sex, or dose after the fact without preregistration risks manufacturing subgroup effects that weren’t there.

The large-and-concentrated reading argues population averages are the wrong lens for a harm that plausibly clusters by developmental window (early puberty), sex, prior vulnerability, and use pattern (passive scrolling versus active use, night-time use), and that a genuinely damaging effect concentrated in a vulnerable minority is exactly what an average washes out: the same logic used for other exposures where subgroup risk, not the population mean, is what drives policy.

questions.text: Is the harm in hours spent, or in engagement-optimized ranking and the content it surfaces?
questions.why: One camp locates the damage in time taken from sleep, play and friendship, the other in what the feed pushes regardless of hours, and the two diagnoses point to different fixes.
questions.detail:
The hours-based case rests on displacement logic: time spent on a screen at night or during unstructured play is time not spent sleeping, moving, or building offline relationships, a mechanism that needs no claim about platform design at all, which is why age- and time-based limits (bans, curfews) are its natural policy answer.

The design-based case points to how engagement-optimized ranking is built to maximize time-on-app and often rewards negative-affect and social-comparison content because that is what drives engagement metrics, arguing two users with identical hours on the same platform can have very different experiences depending on what the feed serves them, which implies the fix is ranking and default regulation (chronological feeds, no autoplay, no engagement-optimized recommendation for minors) rather than a blunt hour or age limit.

questions.text: Does precaution justify restricting a whole age group’s access before causation is established?
questions.why: A burden-of-proof fight: one side treats plausible harm to children as enough to act now, the other treats cutting off a whole age group as itself a serious cost that needs evidence first.
questions.detail:
The precautionary case draws on public-health and product-safety norms, where regulators have restricted access to plausibly harmful products before definitive causal proof, arguing childhood is a uniquely high-stakes, low-reversibility window not to be experimented on while the research catches up. It’s reinforced by parents’ and clinicians’ lived sense that something changed for a generation, independent of what the aggregate statistics can establish so far.

The anti-precaution case treats a blanket age restriction as a real, non-neutral policy that imposes costs today (lost connection, autonomy, and access to peer and support communities, especially for isolated or marginalized youth) on the basis of unresolved science, and warns that precaution has a history of being invoked selectively and outlasting the uncertainty that justified it. It also argues that a felt need to “do something” doesn’t establish that broad restriction is the least-costly response the same evidence base could support.

questions.text: Do school phone bans and national age minimums measurably change what adolescents do or how they feel?
questions.why: Schools report calmer classrooms after a ban, critics expect use to migrate to before and after school, and adoption has run well ahead of rigorous outcome evaluation.
questions.detail:
Supporters point to what schools consistently report after a ban: fewer in-class distractions, instructional time recovered, and more talking in hallways and at lunch. They add that a national age minimum does move behavior at scale rather than merely on paper, with platforms revoking access to about 4.7 million under-16 accounts in the first five weeks of Australia’s law. The claim is that restriction changes the default, and the default is what most adolescents follow.

Skeptics answer that almost none of this is the kind of evidence that settles a causal question: it is largely observational, self-reported or short-horizon, and rarely isolates a ban’s own effect from simultaneous shifts in school culture or enforcement. Their positive reading is displacement, that restricting access in one domain redistributes use rather than reducing it, since determined teens and the platforms both route around a single-point restriction, though displacement too is so far a prediction rather than a measured finding. And the outcomes these policies are ultimately justified by, mood and self-harm indicators, move on a much longer horizon, if at all, than the evaluation windows available so far can capture.

questions.text: Is age-verifying every user an acceptable price for keeping minors off platforms?
questions.why: Enforcing an age floor means checking everyone’s age: either an ID system covering the whole population or a check so porous that minors walk straight past it.
questions.detail:
Parental-authority advocates treat reliable age gating as the precondition every other proposed fix (design rules for minors, access limits) needs in order to actually bind, arguing a check teens can easily evade isn’t a policy at all, and that the privacy cost is manageable with the right technical design, such as attribute-only proofs or third-party verification that never hands the platform an identity document; several push the check down to the app store, so a parent approves once rather than platform by platform.

The anti-verification case argues that age-verification systems tend in practice toward collecting and centralizing sensitive identity data on an entire population to police a fraction of users, creating a durable privacy and surveillance liability, chilling anonymous and adult access alike, while determined minors route around it regardless, so the intervention lands its largest cost on the adults and privacy-conscious users it was never aimed at.

questions.text: How much of the reported rise reflects changed awareness, help-seeking and diagnosis rather than changed distress?
questions.why: Less stigma and more screening raise reported rates on their own, so part of the survey rise may be measuring a greater willingness to name distress rather than more of it.
questions.detail:
The measurement-inflation case notes that the same period saw major public campaigns to destigmatize mental illness, expanded school and clinical screening, and broadened diagnostic categories, all of which mechanically raise reported prevalence with no change required in underlying distress, and argues self-report survey items are especially sensitive to exactly this kind of cultural and definitional shift.

The case against treating this as a major driver notes that harder, less self-report-dependent indicators, such as emergency-department presentations and hospitalization data, have moved in the same direction in some settings, a pattern measurement artifacts alone would not obviously produce; greater willingness to name distress doesn’t by itself explain corroborating signals in institutional-contact data rather than survey wording alone.

positions.name: Great Rewiring Proponent
positions.steelman: Delay the phone, restore play and sleep, and the mental-health curve bends back.
positions.description: Stable minds are built by unsupervised play, in-person friendship and sleep, three things the phone displaced after roughly 2010. Not just a trend line: student mental health worsened campus by campus as Facebook’s mid-2000s rollout reached each one (Braghieri, Levy & Makarin, 2022). The fix is structural: no smartphone before high school, no social media before 16, phone-free schools.
positions.detail:
This case started as a puzzle in the data before it became a book. Jean Twenge argued from national survey data that teenagers born after 1995, the generation she named iGen, looked different from any cohort before them: less time with friends in person, and after 2012 unprecedented levels of anxiety, depression and loneliness, with the break sharpest among girls. Jonathan Haidt, coming at the same numbers as a social psychologist studying moral development and childhood, cross-checked the timing against a separate change nobody was tracking as a health story: the decline of unsupervised outdoor play, which his account dates back to the 1980s. He named the convergence the great rewiring of childhood: a play-based childhood eroding for decades, then giving way in the early 2010s to a phone-based one.

The camp does not rest on the trend lines alone, and its members know the trend lines invite the obvious rebuttal: correlation is not causation. So the case leans harder on convergence than on any single figure: cross-national replication of the same post-2010 break in the UK, Canada, Australia and the Nordic countries, not just the US; a dose-response pattern where heavier users and younger starters fare worst; and quasi-experimental evidence like the staggered US college rollout of Facebook, which let Braghieri, Levy and Makarin isolate a causal effect on mental health from access alone rather than from who chooses to use it. Where the camp splits is on mechanism: Twenge’s data-first wing points at hours displaced from sleep and in-person contact, while Haidt’s wing insists the more precise harm is qualitative, social comparison, algorithmic ranking and interrupted attention, not screen time as such. Both wings agree the fix has to be structural rather than a warning label: age norms and defaults, not individual willpower.

By 2026 the argument has moved well past the seminar room. Haidt and Lenore Skenazy’s Let Grow campaign for restored childhood independence, founded in 2017, predates the book and now runs alongside it; Australia’s under-16 social media law and the UK’s Online Safety Act enforcement draw on the same evidence base, and phone-free school policies have spread from a handful of pilot districts to most of the country, with at least 39 states and the District of Columbia now requiring schools to ban or restrict student phones. The proponents treat that spread as vindication, not overreach: a claim serious enough to change law in multiple countries independently is not a moral panic, it is a diagnosis that finally caught up to what parents and teachers were already seeing at the school gate.
positions.proponents: Jonathan Haidt, Jean Twenge, Zach Rausch, Lenore Skenazy
positions.representative_note: The Anxious Generation (2024) — the synthesis text that turned this case into a mass movement and a four-part policy platform.
positions.prevalence_basis: Legislative and popular footprint: Australia’s under-16 ban in force since December 2025, at least 39 US states and the District of Columbia requiring schools to ban or restrict student phones as of July 2026, and a trade book that has held a place on the New York Times nonfiction best-seller list for more than two years running.

positions.name: Weak Evidence Methodologist
positions.steelman: The effect is the size of eating potatoes, and it shrinks the harder you look.
positions.description: The claim is not that teenagers are fine, but that action must rest on evidence a skeptic cannot take apart. Run every model a fair analyst could defend across three national datasets, 355,000 adolescents, and technology use explains well under half a percent of variation in wellbeing. The 2024 National Academies review agreed: some features look harmful, the population-level causal case is not made.
positions.detail:
Orben and Przybylski applied specification curve analysis, a method introduced by Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, specifically to stop this argument from being settled by whichever single model a researcher happened to run first: instead of one regression, test every combination of predictors, outcomes and covariates a reasonable analyst could defend, then look at the whole distribution of results. Applied across the Monitoring the Future survey, the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System and the UK’s Millennium Cohort Study, roughly 355,000 adolescents in total, nearly every specification landed in the same narrow band: technology use explained well under half a percent of the variance in wellbeing, on the order of the effect of eating potatoes or wearing glasses. That is not one dataset’s quirk; it replicated across three independent, nationally representative samples on two continents.

Sarah Coyne’s eight-year study of 500 US adolescents, surveyed yearly from age 13 to 20, found that increases in an individual teen’s own social media time were not associated with increases in depression or anxiety. The 2024 National Academies consensus study, weighing the literature as a whole rather than one dataset, landed in the same place: some features are plausibly harmful, but the evidence for population-level causation is not there. Chris Ferguson has argued the whole debate is replaying a script familiar from video games, and before that comics and rock music: strong public conviction, thin effect sizes, and a literature that keeps finding less the more rigorously it looks.

None of this says teenagers are thriving or that platforms are beyond reproach; the target is one specific causal story, the one now used to justify age minimums and blanket bans, built largely on unregistered trend lines that move together for one stretch and diverge the next. Odgers has put the alternative plainly: there is a wider set of causes outside social media driving the decline, and a policy built on the shakier claim risks chasing the wrong lever while economic precarity, lost sleep and gutted youth services keep doing the actual damage.
positions.proponents: Amy Orben, Andrew Przybylski, Candice Odgers, Jeff Hancock, Chris Ferguson, Sarah Coyne
positions.representative_note: University of Cambridge (MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit); brought specification-curve analysis to the adolescent wellbeing literature and reset the field’s effect-size expectations
positions.prevalence_basis: Rests on named peer-reviewed work rather than on legislation: Orben and Przybylski’s specification-curve analyses across three national datasets, Coyne and colleagues’ eight-year cohort study of US adolescents, and Candice Odgers’ 2024 Nature review questioning the causal claim.

positions.name: Engagement Design Critic
positions.steelman: Fix the ranking, the autoplay and the notifications, not the age of the user.
positions.description: Connection is not the hazard; engagement-optimized design is. Infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks and ranking tuned to hold attention are doing the damage, and platforms chose to build them. Meta’s own leaked research found roughly one in three teen girls who already felt bad about their bodies said Instagram made it worse. Fix the defaults and the harm falls without taking a phone away.
positions.detail:
Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin’s Time Well Spent movement, which grew into the Center for Humane Technology, first made the design argument mainstream by borrowing a comparison from slot machine research: notifications, infinite scroll and variable-ratio rewards exploit the same psychological mechanisms casinos use, deliberately, to keep a user pulling the lever. Frances Haugen turned that argument from analogy into documented fact when she disclosed thousands of pages of internal Meta research in 2021, showing the company’s own researchers had traced specific harms to specific features, including Instagram’s social comparison and recommendation systems, rather than to time spent in the app. A 2022 investigation by the Center for Countering Digital Hate extended the pattern to TikTok, registering accounts as thirteen-year-olds and finding the recommendation algorithm surfacing suicide and self-harm content within minutes once a viewer lingered on related videos, evidence that the ranking system, not the platform itself, decides how fast a vulnerable user gets pulled toward the worst content available.

The camp splits on how far regulation should go. Design It For Us, a coalition largely made up of the generation being legislated for, argues against blanket age verification on principle: a sixteen-year-old let onto a platform still faces the identical engagement engine, while every user, adult and minor, now hands over identifying documents just to use it. Others in the movement have backed bills that pair design duty-of-care standards with some age-assurance requirements, arguing the two aren’t mutually exclusive so long as the design obligations do the real work. California’s Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, signed in 2022, is the clearest drafted expression of the design-first position, requiring safer default settings and barring manipulative interface patterns aimed at minors without setting an access floor by age at all, though it has spent its whole life in court: enjoined in 2023 and again in 2025, and on 12 March 2026 the Ninth Circuit kept most of it blocked, leaving five of the six challenged provisions enjoined as likely unconstitutional and sending the sixth, age estimation, back to the district court. The camp reads that history as a reason to draft design duties the courts will uphold, not as a reason to abandon the design layer and gate the door instead.

The largest real-world test of the approach arrived by settlement rather than statute. On 26 August 2026 Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of 51 attorneys general for up to $17.1 billion, of which $12.1 billion is guaranteed, over social media harms to children, and a federal judge approved the deal the same day. Meta agreed to change defaults for teen accounts: a two-hour daily limit cumulative across Facebook and Instagram, an overnight cutoff at midnight, notifications muted during school hours, and hidden like counts. The camp reads that as its own agenda reaching the largest platform, defaults and dark patterns rather than an age floor, in the same window its statutes were being enjoined.
positions.proponents: Frances Haugen, Tristan Harris, Aza Raskin, Center for Humane Technology, Design It For Us, Center for Countering Digital Hate, California Age-Appropriate Design Code Act
positions.representative_note: Youth-led coalition pushing platform accountability and safer default design instead of blanket age bans or ID-based age verification.
positions.prevalence_basis: Design-first rules have a real footprint: the UK’s Age Appropriate Design Code, in force since 2021, and the duty-of-care design obligations at the center of the federal kids-online bills, with California’s 2022 Age-Appropriate Design Code Act the drafting model even though the courts have kept it from taking effect, while California’s SB 976 is enforceable in its core: on 9 September 2025 the Ninth Circuit left the state free to enforce its restriction on serving personalized ‘addictive’ feeds to minors without parental consent and its default-private-account requirement, though it blocked the provision hiding like and share counts. Settlement carried the agenda further still: Meta’s agreement with 51 attorneys general on 26 August 2026, worth up to $17.1 billion, imposes default time limits, overnight blocking and hidden like counts on teen accounts.

positions.name: Parental Authority Restorer
positions.steelman: A child needs a parent’s yes to open an account, and the law should make that stick.
positions.description: Parents, not platforms, hold authority over a child’s life, and for two decades the law has let companies contract with minors behind their backs. Restoring it settles no effect-size dispute: a child under 16 should not open an account without a parent’s verified consent, and the parent should be able to withdraw it. Enforce it at the app store, where the age signal already exists.
positions.detail:
This camp’s roots are in family policy rather than developmental psychology, and its argument is jurisdictional: whoever holds the age signal holds the decision. Michael Toscano, who directs the Institute for Family Studies’ Family First Technology Initiative, argues that “parental consent must be the anchor of a child’s power to access a social media account,” and that verification therefore has to be applied at two levels, the platform and the app store, so a single check at the point of download covers every app a child installs instead of leaving each service to run its own gate.

That design is now law in several states. Texas enacted its App Store Accountability Act in May 2025, effective January 2026, and Utah has enacted an act of its own, requiring app stores to establish a user’s age band and obtain parental consent before a minor downloads an app. The coalition behind it, Focus on the Family, the Texas Public Policy Foundation and a bipartisan group of state attorneys general, is opposed by Apple, Google, the Computer & Communications Industry Association and R Street, whose objection is precisely that the app store is the wrong chokepoint. So far the route has held: on 6 July 2026 the Supreme Court denied emergency applications from the Computer & Communications Industry Association and a student group to vacate the stay shielding the Texas act, leaving age checks and parental consent for app downloads enforceable while the litigation continues.

Where this camp parts from the developmental case is what the evidence has to prove. It does not need a settled causal estimate for social media’s effect on adolescent wellbeing, because its claim is about who decides for a child, not about how much harm a study can measure; and where the design critics would regulate ranking for everyone, this camp is content to leave adult feeds alone. Its own internal split is over the fallback: some members treat app-store verification as sufficient, while others want platform-level checks too, on the grounds that a child who borrows a signed-in device walks straight past the store.
positions.proponents: Michael Toscano, Institute for Family Studies (Family First Technology Initiative), Digital Childhood Alliance, American Principles Project, National Center on Sexual Exploitation, Texas Public Policy Foundation, Focus on the Family
positions.representative_note: Directs the Institute for Family Studies’ Family First Technology Initiative; argued in August 2026 that parental consent must be the anchor of a child’s access, verified at both the platform and the app-store level.
positions.prevalence_basis: App Store Accountability Acts enacted in Texas (May 2025, effective January 2026) and Utah, left enforceable when the Supreme Court declined on 6 July 2026 to block the Texas act, plus family-policy organizations and a bipartisan group of state attorneys general pressing platforms and app stores on parental consent, against opposition from Apple, Google and the app-store trade associations.

positions.name: Vulnerable Subgroup Researcher
positions.steelman: The average is small because it averages away who is actually being hurt.
positions.description: The question was never how big the average effect is, but which teenagers are affected, when, and by how much. Across 2,155 real-time reports from Dutch adolescents, 44% felt no different after passive social media use, 46% felt better and 10% felt worse: a near-zero average built from people it fits badly. Support belongs on the children actually affected, not on a blanket verdict.
positions.detail:
Long before smartphones, communication researchers already knew that media-effects debates asking “how big is the effect of X on everyone” were badly specified. Valkenburg and Peter’s Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model, formalized in 2013, argued that any media effect is conditional on dispositional, developmental and social differences between individuals, so a single population average describes nobody in particular. When the post-2010 phone debate collapsed into a fight over point estimates, Orben and Przybylski’s specification-curve analysis putting technology use at no more than 0.4% of the variation in adolescent well-being, against larger figures from researchers pooling cruder measures, this camp read both sides as chasing the same wrong number from opposite directions.

The stronger test swaps the one-off survey for repeated, person-specific measurement. Beyens and colleagues’ 2020 study in Scientific Reports is the field’s clearest demonstration: six-times-daily experience-sampling over a week, 2,155 real-time assessments, found that after passive social media use 44% of the adolescents felt no different, 46% felt better and 10% felt worse, a spread the group average erases entirely. Orben, Przybylski, Blakemore and Kievit’s later analysis of a large UK longitudinal cohort located a second axis inside the same heterogeneity: the same hour of daily use predicted meaningfully lower life satisfaction a year later specifically in the years bracketing puberty, with a further dip around age nineteen and little association in between. Neither paper found a big flat effect; both found structure, exactly where the population-average approach is built not to look.

The camp’s live disagreement is what “vulnerable” should mean for policy. One wing follows Orben’s developmental-timing evidence toward protections keyed to puberty rather than a flat legal age. Another, closer to Nesi’s work on co-rumination and social comparison, argues the stronger predictor is pre-existing risk, depression, low self-esteem, prior bullying, which points toward clinical screening embedded in schools and pediatric care rather than a platform-wide age gate that protects a majority who were never at risk while doing comparatively little for the minority who are. Both wings agree on the same complaint against the rest of the debate: a single average effect size was never going to settle this, because it was never measuring the thing that matters.
positions.proponents: Patti Valkenburg, Amy Orben, Ine Beyens, Jacqueline Nesi, Rogier Kievit
positions.representative_note: Developed the Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model, then tested it directly: her lab’s 2020 experience-sampling study found no average effect but sharply different effects, in both directions, in the individuals the average erased.
positions.prevalence_basis: Rests on the person-specific-effects literature: Valkenburg and Peter’s differential-susceptibility model, Beyens and colleagues’ experience-sampling study in Scientific Reports, and Orben and colleagues’ windows-of-sensitivity analysis in Nature Communications.

positions.name: Digital Rights Defender
positions.steelman: Age gates don’t protect minors; they lock out the ones who need connection most.
positions.description: Minors are rights-holders: the Supreme Court struck down California’s video-game age law because they keep “a significant measure” of First Amendment protection. Age checks make every user, adult or child, hand an ID or face scan to vendors already breached. Those shut out have the least elsewhere: 68% of LGBTQ+ youth call online spaces affirming, against 52% for school and 40% for home.
positions.detail:
The digital-rights argument didn’t start with social media, it precedes it: danah boyd’s ethnographic work with American teens in the 2000s and 2010s argued that shrinking unsupervised physical space (curfews, structured schedules, driving restrictions, fear-driven parenting) pushed adolescent social life online, so platforms became the mall and the park rolled into one screen. Cutting off access doesn’t restore the old commons; it just removes the substitute teens actually have. When state legislatures started passing the age-verification and parental-consent laws that family-authority campaigners had been drafting, through 2022 to 2024, NetChoice’s industry suits carried the litigation, with EFF and the ACLU filing amicus briefs alongside them and Fight for the Future organizing against the bills in the legislatures; federal judges blocked laws in Arkansas and California, holding that minors cannot be walled off from lawful speech wholesale.

The camp is not naive about platform harms; it splits from the precaution camp on the remedy, not the diagnosis. Its strongest evidence is about who loses the pathway when the door closes, not about pathology: the Trevor Project’s 2024 survey found 68% of LGBTQ+ young people describe online spaces as affirming, against 52% for school and 40% for home, and separately that past-year attempt rates fall from 20% among those in very unaccepting communities to 8% among those in very accepting ones. The camp reads that pairing as naming exactly the population an ID-gated internet locks out first, since these are also the youth least likely to find acceptance at home or at school. The privacy half runs alongside: every age-verification scheme requires a government ID or biometric face scan from every user, not just minors, handed to third-party verification vendors that have already suffered breaches, manufacturing a mass-surveillance infrastructure to solve a problem, engagement-optimized design, that has nothing to do with anyone’s age.

Where the camp disagrees internally is how far to push. Some, echoing Brown v. EMA’s deference logic, favor near-total protection for platforms and parental choice over legislative content rules. Others, including EFF staff like David Greene and Daly Barnett, accept narrower defaults (privacy settings safer by default, no design features that target minors specifically) as long as they stop short of identity checks at the door. What unites both wings is the refusal to trade a named population’s privacy and speech for an unproven safety claim, and a preference for suing over laws after they pass rather than waiting to be asked.
positions.proponents: Electronic Frontier Foundation, ACLU, Center for Democracy & Technology, Fight for the Future, danah boyd
positions.representative_note: Director of Fight for the Future; led national opposition to the Kids Online Safety Act, warning its duty-of-care and age-assurance provisions would push platforms toward mandatory ID checks and content policing of LGBTQ+ and reproductive-health information.
positions.prevalence_basis: Courts are the footprint: a federal judge partly blocked Nebraska’s age-verification law on 29 June 2026, on top of the earlier Arkansas and California blocks, with EFF, ACLU and NetChoice litigating across more than a dozen states. Those wins are against platform-level statutes; the app-store route has proved harder to stop, with the December 2025 federal injunction against Texas’s App Store Accountability Act on appeal and the law’s age checks enforceable while the challenge proceeds.

positions.name: Media Skills Clinician
positions.steelman: The question was never how much, but how, and how can be taught.
positions.description: Children respond to social media differently, so the question is not how many hours but what those hours do to this child. The American Academy of Pediatrics swapped flat screen-time limits for the 5 Cs of Media Use, a Family Media Plan and clinician screening. An age floor treats a twelve-year-old messaging a friend and one scrolling at midnight alike; skills tell them apart.
positions.detail:
The lineage here is clinical rather than legislative. The American Academy of Pediatrics spent years issuing flat screen-time limits and then moved away from them: its Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health, funded by SAMHSA and co-directed by pediatricians Megan Moreno and Jenny Radesky, now frames the digital media guidelines around a child’s overall well-being rather than an hour count, with socio-ecological thinking and child-centered design as the organizing concepts. The premise is stated on the Center’s own front page: the connection between social media and mental health is complicated and personal, and everyone responds to social media differently. That is not a hedge. It is the reason a population average cannot tell a pediatrician what to do on a Tuesday afternoon with one particular fourteen-year-old.

What the camp offers in place of a rule is a practice. The 5 Cs of Media Use give clinicians a framework for starting the conversation and building skills; the Family Media Plan lets a family set its own priorities, screen-free times and screen-free places; motivational interviewing training helps providers work with a family instead of issuing instructions to it; and screening and intervention tools exist for problematic media use, treated as a pattern some children develop rather than a property every platform has for everyone. A Teen Wellness Toolkit, a glossary of the platforms children actually use, a set of screen-free coping strategies and an early-childhood toolkit carry the same logic out to teens, families and preschool settings.

The camp is not against structure, and that is where it splits internally. Its own Youth Advisory Panel publishes advice for policymakers and separate advice for the tech industry, and the Center has published research on how parents’ messaging shapes whether students break a school phone policy, which points toward working alongside school rules and platform design rather than only around them. One wing treats guidance and screening as the whole intervention; another accepts bans and design mandates as a floor, so long as the skills work happens on top of them. What unites them is the objection to the shape of the argument: a fight over how much is a fight over the wrong variable, and the variable that is actually movable in a clinic room is how.
positions.proponents: American Academy of Pediatrics Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health, Megan Moreno, Jenny Radesky
positions.representative_name: AAP Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health
positions.representative_note: The federally funded national center, co-directed by pediatricians Megan Moreno and Jenny Radesky, that publishes the 5 Cs of Media Use, the Family Media Plan and clinician screening tools in place of age floors or flat time limits.
positions.prevalence_basis: The footprint is clinical rather than legislative: a SAMHSA-funded national center at the American Academy of Pediatrics, standing where the Academy’s flat screen-time limits used to be, whose 5 Cs of Media Use, Family Media Plan and problematic-media-use screening tools reach families through routine pediatric practice and HealthyChildren.org.

positions.name: Social Determinants Camp
positions.steelman: Distress tracks the rent, the workload and the therapist waitlist, not the screen.
positions.description: Adolescent distress is real; calling it a technology problem lets policymakers off the hook for economic insecurity, academic pressure, lost sleep and gutted clinics. Youth-service funding in England has fallen 76% in real terms since 2010–11, a £1.3 billion loss, over the decade credited to phones. Blame the phone and the fix is a parental control; blame the rent and the fix is policy.
positions.detail:
Start with the timeline critics of the phone hypothesis keep pointing to: the Great Recession hit in 2008, foreclosures and long-term unemployment scarred the cohort entering parenthood, and the children born into that instability are the same generation now showing up in the distress statistics. Where the rewiring story reads 2012 as the year the smartphone rewired childhood, this camp reads the same decade as the one in which austerity-era cuts to youth services, early-intervention programs and school counseling finally showed up in outcomes, because funding cuts take years to bite.

The camp does not deny the phone is present in adolescents’ lives, only that its presence is doing the causal work claimed for it when other, better-measured stressors moved in the same decade. Academic pressure intensified as college admissions grew more competitive, and Denise Pope’s Challenge Success project at Stanford, which works with schools on exactly this, puts homework load, testing and the scramble for admission at the center of student stress. Sleep loss tracks early school start times and after-school jobs as much as bedtime scrolling. And in both the US and UK, child and adolescent mental health services were left so underfunded that a referred teenager often waits months for a first appointment, turning a treatable episode into a chronic one.

Internally, the camp splits over emphasis. Economists in the Case-and-Deaton tradition foreground labor-market precarity and a generation facing higher housing costs and more debt than their parents. UK-focused advocates like YoungMinds foreground the collapse of the service infrastructure that used to catch distress early. Epidemiologists like Katherine Keyes foreground academic and social pressure cohort effects layered on top. What unites them against the rewiring narrative is a refusal to let a technology story substitute for a policy story: the proposed fix is not a parental control, but investment, in youth services, in affordable housing, and in school systems that stopped treating sixteen-year-olds like junior professionals competing for a shrinking number of slots.
positions.proponents: Candice Odgers, Anne Case, Angus Deaton, Katherine Keyes, Denise Pope, YoungMinds
positions.representative_note: UC Irvine psychologist whose March 2024 Nature review of The Anxious Generation argued that guns, violence, structural racism, the opioid epidemic and economic hardship better explain the post-2010 trends than social media.
positions.prevalence_basis: Carried by researchers and service providers rather than by legislation: Candice Odgers’ 2024 Nature review pressing this case against the phone-based-childhood account, Case and Deaton’s deaths-of-despair work on the economic roots of distress, and YMCA England & Wales’ analysis of the 76% real-terms collapse in English youth-services funding.

positions.name: Prevalence Inflation Theorist
positions.steelman: Not all distress is new: some of it was always there, only now it has a name.
positions.description: Destigmatization worked: teenagers have language and screening earlier generations lacked, and using them is not itself evidence of decline. Foulkes and Andrews’ 2023 prevalence inflation hypothesis names the mechanism: awareness lowers the bar for what counts as a problem and invites self-labeling of mild states. The distress is real; a 2010 survey category and a 2024 one may not match.
positions.detail:
Foulkes and Andrews did not claim to have proven prevalence inflation when they named it in 2023; they called it a hypothesis and challenged the field to test it, laying out the mechanisms it would predict: overinterpretation of normal distress, self-fulfilling labeling effects, and a lowered bar for what counts as impairment. That posture, hypothesis rather than verdict, is itself part of the case: precaution advocates rarely extend the same evidentiary caution to the trend they are trying to explain.

The camp is careful about which numbers it actually contests. Self-harm hospitalizations and completed suicide, the hardest indicators because they do not depend on how a teenager chooses to describe their own inner state, also climbed over the same period, and most serious proponents concede those figures are not primarily an artifact of labeling. The inflation argument targets the softer end of the distribution: screening-survey positives, self-identified diagnoses, and subclinical distress, where Haslam’s decades of concept creep research shows categories such as trauma, bullying, and abuse have both broadened to new phenomena and crept downward to catch milder instances of old ones.

Proponents also lean on an old distinction psychiatric epidemiology has never resolved: a brief self-report screener and a structured clinical interview do not identify the same people, and a screening positive is not a diagnosis. Nobody ran that comparison on the adolescent surveys before the headlines about a mental health epidemic went out, they argue, so the possibility that the gap between screening and diagnosis is doing some of the work in the youth trend has barely been tested.
positions.proponents: Lucy Foulkes, Jack L. Andrews, Nick Haslam
positions.representative_name: Lucy Foulkes and Jack L. Andrews
positions.representative_note: Their 2023 paper in New Ideas in Psychology coined the term and framed the mechanism as a testable hypothesis rather than a settled finding, the field’s most careful statement of the case.
positions.prevalence_basis: Footprint is a 2023 paper in New Ideas in Psychology by Lucy Foulkes and Jack Andrews, Foulkes’ 2024 trade book Coming of Age, and UK media commentary.

crux.lead: Everyone is reading the same average, and no two camps agree on what it is an average of.
crux.lead_highlight: what it is an average of
crux.subtitle: The same number reads as no effect, as a real cause measured crudely, or as harm concentrated in a few children; and for two camps its size is beside the point, since the fight is over who decides.
crux.empirical: Much is settleable: whether preregistered within-person designs recover an effect once confounding and self-report error are handled; whether harm concentrates by age, dose and vulnerability; whether ranking changes move outcomes independently of hours; whether bans and age minimums shift behavior or mood; how much of the rise survives changed diagnosis.
crux.values: Evidence cannot fix the burden of proof. How much certainty precaution owes before an entire age group loses access, whether a minority harmed badly outweighs a majority mildly affected, whether minors’ privacy and speech and everyone’s identity check are an acceptable price, and who gets to define disorder, are commitments, not findings.

actions.title: Take action for a phone-free childhood
actions.description: Jonathan Haidt’s Anxious Generation movement offers parents, educators and students petitions, action guides and templates to delay smartphones and social media and make local schools phone-free bell-to-bell.

actions.title: Read the National Academies report
actions.description: A 2024 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine consensus study finding some social media features plausibly harmful but the evidence for population-level causation still unsettled, and calling for more rigorous causal research before broad restrictions.

actions.title: Join the Design It For Us coalition
actions.description: A youth-led coalition organizing to hold platforms accountable for engagement-driven design and to pass algorithmic-accountability legislation, rather than gate access by age.

actions.title: Follow the family-first technology agenda
actions.description: The Institute for Family Studies’ Family First Technology Initiative, directed by Michael Toscano, researches how technology affects families, drafts model parental-consent legislation, and has filed Supreme Court briefs supporting state app-store age-verification laws; it publishes a family policy briefing and welcomes supporters.

actions.title: Explore the windows-of-sensitivity research
actions.description: University of Cambridge research led by Amy Orben found social media’s association with lower wellbeing concentrated in specific ages and puberty stages (girls 11-13, boys 14-15) rather than spread evenly across adolescence.

actions.title: Tell Congress: reject KOSA’s privacy risks
actions.description: The Electronic Frontier Foundation argues the Kids Online Safety Act would push platforms toward sweeping age verification and chill lawful speech, and asks supporters to contact Congress to oppose it.

actions.title: Build a family media plan
actions.description: The American Academy of Pediatrics’ Family Media Plan, on HealthyChildren.org, walks a family through setting its own media priorities, screen-free times and screen-free places instead of applying a flat hour limit.

actions.title: Support economic security for children
actions.description: First Focus on Children advocates for anti-poverty policy such as the Child Tax Credit and tracks federal investment in children through its annual Children’s Budget analysis, addressing the material pressures this position points to.

actions.title: Read the prevalence inflation case
actions.description: Oxford psychologist Lucy Foulkes argues in the British Journal of Psychiatry that mental health awareness efforts may be inflating reported distress by encouraging young people to label mild, transient symptoms as disorder.

actions.title: Add your view
actions.description: Share your own take on smartphones, social media and youth mental health.
